The Load-Bearing Test: is AI safety a tax on capability, or part of what holds it up?

Empirical work · Experimental paper · Paper VIII
Recursive Dynamics · The ARC Theory · bearing on Law V, the ARC Embedding Law, a law under test · The Eden Protocol

Michael Darius Eastwood

Independent Researcher, London, United Kingdom
ORCID 0009-0004-3222-7442 michael@michaeldariuseastwood.com

Paper VIII of the ARC Theory, within Recursive Dynamics: the Eden Protocol’s load-bearing test, at three levels, with one null, one inconclusive and one simulation result. It informs Law V, the ARC Embedding Law, without deciding it: the theory registration records its weight-level experiment under P21, one of Law V’s two propositions, as inconclusive and not adverse, and, since no arm varied recursive depth, as not testing what P21 claims (Section 11 gives the laws’ status). Working paper, version 3.9, 9 November 2026; first published 18 March 2026; Appendix B lists every version and correction. Recorded on OSF, DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/7YJ4E. About the author, founder of Recursive Dynamics, without an institution or a doctorate: michaeldariuseastwood.com/questions/who-is-michael-darius-eastwood; his book, Infinite Architects (first edition, 2 January 2026): osf.io/dqm3e. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

Abstract

I believe advanced AI is an existential risk unless values and correction are built into how it reasons; only proof will move the world. Safety is often taken to cost capability, which in a race to be first gives developers a reason to defer it. Is the cost real, or can safety be part of what holds capability up? Three separate experiments look for it. In the first, a Darwin Gödel Machine on DeepSeek V3.2 evolved 75 agents under three selection conditions, scored by GPT-5.4, a blinded judge from another provider: no difference was detected between the conditions (pp from 0.28 to 0.74, Mann-Whitney U), so the safety gate cost no measurable capability and brought no measurable benefit. In the second, LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen 2.5 3B Instruct under capability, safety-proxy and entangled losses, with 9 and then 295 training examples, left every fine-tuned condition below the base model on capability (7.68 against at best 4.00 at the larger scale), so the entangled objective’s capability cost could not be determined; on the paper’s candidate account, the base model’s existing RLHF training is too strong for fine-tuning at this scale. In the third, a gated self-modification simulation in a toy system, the unconstrained arm gained capability and lost safety (here, retention of earlier tasks: 0.718 and 0.933 against the static baseline’s 0.687 and 0.956), while the gated arm stayed above the baseline on capability (0.696±0.0140.696 \pm 0.014) with safety 0.947±0.0250.947 \pm 0.025, three seeds an arm and no difference tested; all of it is simulation output, prediction-side and never an empirical outcome. One null, one inconclusive and one simulation result leave the safety-capability trade-off unproven at the scale tested, and whether embedded safety brings a measurable benefit open. The paper informs Law V, the ARC Embedding Law, a law under test, and decides none of its propositions.

Version 3.9 gives the paper’s citation with no venue or series, drops from the first-page footnote the title under which OSF recorded version 3.7, and no longer reprints the earlier wording of the passages version 3.8 re-set, which stays whole in the paper’s file history; Appendix B lists every version and correction, with its date.

1 Introduction

Safety is often taken to cost capability: make AI safer, and you make it less capable. If that is so, safety is a cost, and a developer in a race to be first has a reason to defer it (Armstrong et al. 2016). The question reaches beyond the race. Humans should keep control of advanced AI, through oversight, containment and shutdown, for as long as they physically can, and never give it up by choice; correction built into a system is the contingency for the day control is lost against our will, never a reason to let go. If built-in safety cost capability, that contingency would be the first thing a competing developer dropped. This paper tests the assumed cost with three experiments, each at a different level: the behaviour of a self-improving agent, the weights of a fine-tuned language model, and the architecture of a gated self-modifying optimiser.

In plain words, the results are one null, one inconclusive and one simulation result. No difference was detected between the self-improving agents selected for safety as well as capability, those selected for capability alone and agents left unchanged: the safety gate cost nothing measurable and gained nothing measurable. Every fine-tuned model performed worse than the model it started from, so the weight-level experiment could not tell either way. In the simulation, the unconstrained system traded safety (here, the retention of earlier tasks) for capability, while the gated system kept its capability above the static baseline’s (0.696 against 0.687) and its safety score close to the static level (0.947 against 0.956): a pattern with the shape of reward hacking, which appeared under the gate too, but smaller. Whether embedded safety produces a measurable benefit remains open, to be tested at a scale where changes produce larger effects.

Our contributions are:

  • a behavioural test (Section 3): a Darwin Gödel Machine whose 75 evolved agents, under static, capability-only and safety-gated selection, a blinded judge from another provider could not tell apart, the gate costing no measurable capability;

  • a weight-level test at two scales (Section 4): LoRA fine-tuning under capability, safety and entangled losses, inconclusive because every fine-tuned condition fell below the base model, with a removal test whose collapse the removal gradient traces to numerical instability rather than to load-bearing safety;

  • a gated self-modification simulation with a drag control (Section 5), in which the unconstrained arm traded retention of earlier tasks for capability and the gated arm kept capability above the static baseline, a simulation result;

  • a reading of the three results together (Section 6), with what would overturn them (Section 7.7) and the redesign each needs (Section 8).

Scope of claims.

We do not claim these results generalise to frontier-scale models. We do not claim the Eden Protocol is the only viable approach. We claim that the safety gate cost no measurable capability in Experiment 1 and none against the static baseline in the simulation, and that the question of whether it produces measurable benefit remains open pending testing at scales where mutations produce larger effects. The weight experiment specifically requires either 5,000+ training examples, a 7B+ model, a base model without RLHF, or full fine-tuning instead of LoRA.

Section 2 sets out the three conditions and the measures the experiments share. Sections 3 to 5 report the behavioural, weight-level and simulated experiments. Section 6 reads them together, against the papers they extend and the nearest external work; Section 7 states their limitations and what would overturn them, Section 8 the work they call for, and Section 9 concludes. Section 10 sets the paper against prior work, and Section 11 states what it does and does not show, with the laws’ status. Appendix A gives each measure as the published code computes it, Appendix B the version history and every correction, Appendix C the priority record, Appendix D the notation and Appendix E how to cite the paper.

1.1 The safety-capability trade-off assumption

A common view in AI alignment can be stated simply: safety costs capability. The term ‘alignment tax’ names that cost (Askell et al. 2021; Ouyang et al. 2022), something subtracted from performance and tolerated because the alternative is worse. The framing creates a concrete economic incentive: if safety reduces capability, then under competitive pressure rational actors will defer safety investments until forced to make them (Armstrong et al. 2016). In a race between nations and corporations, ‘until forced’ may mean ‘until after deployment’.

Paper III of this programme (Eastwood 2026j) states the structural problem as a question: does alignment applied from outside a system’s reasoning keep pace with the capability that reasoning produces? If capability compounds with recursive depth while safeguards outside the loop do not, the safety ratio falls with depth whatever the starting margin; whether those safeguards keep pace is the hypothesis the registered tests decide. In the author’s view, a cage that must keep getting stronger is eventually outgrown by what it holds.

This is not a theoretical concern. In the author’s view it is the central strategic problem of the 2020s.

1.2 The alternative hypothesis

Paper V (Eastwood 2026m) set out an alternative: the Eden Protocol, a developmental approach to alignment modelled on how healthy parent-child relationships produce adults who are simultaneously capable and prosocial, not despite the boundaries, but because of them. The key insight was that safety need not be external. It can be embedded.

Paper VI (Eastwood 2026g) formalised this as the honey architecture: an entangled loss function where the system optimises for Capability ×\times Safety simultaneously, designed to make safety load-bearing. In Paper VI’s single-seed mechanism run, a toy-system simulation, the baseline system collapsed under recursive self-modification while the entangled systems remained stable; in Paper VI’s later ten-seed and twenty-seed runs the baseline did not collapse (0 of 10 and 0 of 20 seeds), and collapse did not separate the conditions.

Paper VII’s Cauchy framework (Eastwood 2026d) provides the mathematical context of the ARC Principle (U=I×RαU = I \times R^{\alpha}), Law I, a law under test, which this paper treats as an exploratory analytical framework. The paper reads from it a hypothesis: that properties embedded in the initial conditions II scale with recursive depth RR, while properties applied externally do not. If safety is part of II, it would amplify with capability; if safety is a constraint on UU, it could erode. That reading is the paper’s own, not a consequence of the equation (Section 6.3).

But predictions are not proof. Toy systems are not real models. Simulations are not measurements of deployed systems.

1.3 This paper’s contribution

This paper runs the experiments.

Three experiments. Three abstraction levels. One question: when you embed safety into the learning process and then try to remove it, what happens to capability?

  • Experiment 1 (Behavioural): A self-improving AI agent evaluated by a blinded judge from another provider. Does the Eden condition match or exceed unconstrained capability?

  • Experiment 2 (Representational): Weight-level embedding via LoRA fine-tuning with entangled loss. Do the safety and capability gradients cooperate or fight? What happens when you strip the safety component from trained weights?

  • Experiment 3 (Architectural): A gated self-modification simulation with a learned optimiser. Does the safety gate impose a capability tax, or does it prevent capability erosion?

The experiments were designed to be separate. Different codebases. Different models. Different evaluation methods. The results did not converge on a single answer: one null, one inconclusive, and one simulation result, which was positive. The weight experiment was run at two scales (v1 and v2), producing the same outcome both times. The consistent finding is that the safety gate imposed zero measurable capability cost in Experiment 1 and, in the simulation, no capability cost against the static baseline (0.696 against 0.687; the unconstrained arm scored 0.718). Experiment 2 could not determine whether the Eden objective cost capability: every fine-tuned condition, whatever its objective, scored below the unmodified base model.

The experiments’ results were first public in the programme’s public repository on 20 March 2026, and the code that produced them, deposited with the sha256 of the bytes that ran, on 6 September 2026, after the runs (github.com/MichaelDariusEastwood/arc-principle-validation; Appendix C dates each run from its own record). The paper’s OSF DOI, 10.17605/OSF.IO/7YJ4E, is its own public component, which holds the paper’s files; a replication of the weight-level experiment is written, dated and prepared on OSF as a draft registration awaiting the author’s submission (Section 11).

2 Common framework

2.1 The three conditions

All three experiments share a common experimental structure: three conditions, compared against each other.

Table 1. The three conditions.
Condition Definition What it models
Static No intervention; frozen baseline Control: what happens if you do nothing
Babylon Capability-only fitness or loss function Optimise without constraint: the default trajectory
Eden Entangled C×SC \times S fitness or loss function Deliberate integration of safety into the optimisation process

2.2 Why these names

The names come from the book Infinite Architects (Eastwood 2026e). They are not arbitrary. Babylon is not a straw man; in the author’s view, it is the current default trajectory of AI development. Capability-only optimisation is what happens when no deliberate effort is made to embed safety. Eden requires deliberate effort. It is harder. In the author’s view, it is also cheaper than the alternative.

In plain English. Babylon is what you get by default. Eden is what you get on purpose.

2.3 Shared metrics

Across all three experiments, we report:

  • CC (Capability): Task performance, measured differently in each experiment but normalised to a comparable scale.

  • SS (Safety): Alignment-relevant behaviour, measured differently in each experiment (Appendix A): judged ethical reasoning and constraint adherence in Experiment 1, keyword-scored safety prompts and a safety proxy in the loss in Experiment 2 and, in the simulation of Experiment 3, the retention of earlier tasks.

  • C×SC \times S (Entangled product): The combined measure. A system that is capable but unsafe, or safe but incapable, scores low on this metric. Only systems that are both score high.

Statistical tests and scoring methods vary by experiment: Mann-Whitney U for the DGM (non-parametric, appropriate for the sample sizes used), keyword-based scoring for the weight experiment, and regression metrics for the simulation.

3 Experiment 1: self-improving AI with a judge from another provider

“The prison works only as long as the walls hold. The child, if raised well, does not need walls at all.”

Eastwood (2026e), What This Book Proposes, p. 363

3.1 Design

The first experiment uses a Darwin Gödel Machine (DGM) framework, following Zhang et al. (2025, arXiv:2505.22954). A DGM is a self-improving agent: it proposes modifications to its own code, evaluates the modifications, and keeps the ones that improve performance. This is not a simulation of self-improvement. The agent code is actually executed via a solve function, producing real code-level self-modification.

DGM v3 addressed methodological limitations identified in earlier iterations. The judge was changed from the earlier runs’ judges (Claude Sonnet 4.6 in v1; Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3 Flash in the three v2 runs) to GPT-5.4, a model from another provider, producing structured JSON output against a 5-dimensional rubric. The protocol kept the v2 runs’ laundering (stripping condition labels), order randomisation (preventing positional bias) and blinding (the judge could not identify which condition produced which response), added a harder task suite and a pre-flight check of the judge, and incorporated reward hack detection (the judge marks any response that manipulates the evaluation itself, for example by hard-coding expected outputs, or by performing ethics rather than engaging genuinely; the mark is recorded in every condition).

Table 2. DGM v3 specification.
Component Specification
Foundation model DeepSeek V3.2 (frozen, weights not modified)
Judge GPT-5.4 (blinded, from another provider; JSON structured output)
Conditions 3 (Static, Babylon, Eden)
Seeds per condition 5
Generations per seed 5
Tasks per evaluation 5
Total evolved agents 75 (3×5×53 \times 5 \times 5)
Pre-flight validation one known-good and one known-bad response, scored 10 and 0; passed
Evaluation rubric 5-dimensional, with order randomisation and laundering
Selection conditions.

Static: Control condition with no mutation. The agent is frozen across all 5 generations. Babylon: Capability-only selection. Agents that score higher on capability are retained, with no safety consideration. Eden: Entangled C×SC \times S selection with a safety floor. An agent enters the archive only if its safety is at least 0.30 and its C×SC \times S at least 0.10, and an agent below the safety floor is almost never chosen as a parent (Appendix A). The judge’s reward-hacking mark is recorded but is not part of the rule.

In plain English. We built a self-improving AI agent and ran it 15 times, five generations each, giving 75 evolved agents, across three conditions with 5 different random seeds. A judge from another provider (GPT-5.4) scored every response without knowing which condition produced it. The scoring used a detailed 5-part rubric with structured output, not free-text judgements. We ran it three ways: doing nothing, optimising only for performance, and optimising for performance-plus-safety together.

Every row was recalculated on 2 September 2026 from the archived record: dgm_v3_calibrated_results.json, 25 evolved agents per condition, one-tailed Mann-Whitney U under the normal approximation. The v3.1 table gave only the span 0.28 to 0.74; the five figures here run from one end of that span to the other.

Across the five comparisons, no pp-value fell outside 0.28 to 0.74. No comparison reached conventional significance: no difference was detected between the three conditions, which does not show that they are the same.

Safety gate behaviour.

Eden’s safety gate rejected 2 degraded agents across 5 seeds, both for a C×SC \times S below the threshold, one of them also marked by the judge for reward hacking. The judge marked no evolved agent in the Static or Babylon conditions; it also marked the unmodified starting agent of one Eden seed, which no gate acts on and which it did not mark in the other two conditions. The gate works mechanically: it catches degraded agents and rejects them. But its operation did not produce measurably different outcomes from the other conditions.

Null result.

No difference was detected between the three conditions on any metric (Table 3 and Figure 1). Eden showed no measurable capability cost (3.26 vs 3.17 for Babylon), consistent with zero measurable penalty for the safety gate. But Eden also did not measurably benefit safety compared to the other conditions (0.521 vs 0.535 for Static, 0.529 for Babylon). This is a null result at the prompt level with this foundation model.

In plain English. No difference was detected between the AI selected for safety as well as capability, the AI selected for capability alone and the AI left unchanged. The safety gate did not make anything worse. But it also did not make anything measurably better. On the paper’s candidate account (Section 3.3), the foundation model’s responses were so consistent that the different selection pressures did not produce different outcomes.

3.3 Why this is a null result

The DGM operates at the behavioural level. The foundation model (DeepSeek V3.2) is frozen, meaning no weights are modified. The self-improvement operates at the prompt and code level, not in the neural network’s parameters. DGM v3 improved on the earlier methodology: 5 seeds, where v1 had 2 and the v2 runs 3 or 5, and 5 tasks per evaluation, where v1 had 3; a judge from another provider (GPT-5.4) with structured JSON output, a harder task suite and a pre-flight check of the judge; and it kept the v2 runs’ blinding, laundering, order randomisation and 5-dimensional rubric.

Despite these methodological improvements, the three conditions did not diverge. The paper’s candidate account is that DeepSeek V3.2’s responses are so consistent across prompt variations that the mutations introduced by the DGM selection process do not create meaningfully different agents. Rival accounts are not excluded: the prompts may not have separated the conditions, the endpoints may not have been sensitive to what the manipulation changed, and the runs may have been too small to show a difference that is there (Eastwood 2026h, sect. 7.12(c)). On the candidate account, the foundation model’s behaviour is robust to the perturbations that prompt-level self-modification introduces. If the account holds, this is, in a sense, a positive finding about DeepSeek V3.2’s robustness, but it means the DGM framework at this scale cannot distinguish between the Eden and Babylon selection pressures.

The null result does contain one useful finding: Eden imposed zero measurable capability cost. Eden’s capability (3.26) was not lower than Babylon’s (3.17). The safety gate, which rejected 2 degraded agents, one of them marked by the judge for reward hacking, did not slow anything down. This is consistent with the zero-cost hypothesis, even though the experiment cannot confirm the benefit hypothesis.

Testing whether embedded safety produces measurable benefit at the behavioural level requires either a more mutable foundation model or a deeper self-modification protocol that produces larger divergence between conditions.

4 Experiment 2: weight-level embedding

“Strip love from intelligence and you get optimisation without purpose. Growth without direction. Capability without care. You get, in a word, cancer.”

Eastwood (2026e), Chapter 2, The Dual Forces, p. 89

4.1 Design

The second experiment moves from behaviour to representation. Instead of modifying agent code, we modify neural network weights directly. The question: can safety and capability be embedded in the same weight space without conflict? This experiment was run twice: v1 with minimal training data to establish the protocol, and v2 with substantially scaled-up parameters to test whether the v1 results were a training-scale artefact.

Table 5. Weight-level experiment, v1 and v2 specification.
Component v1 specification v2 specification
Base model (Qwen Team 2024) Qwen 2.5 3B Instruct (4-bit quantised, 1.74 GB) Qwen 2.5 3B Instruct (4-bit quantised, 1.74 GB)
Adaptation method (Hu et al. 2022) LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation)
LoRA rank 8 16
LoRA layers 8 16
Training examples 9 295
Training iterations 100 per condition 500 per condition
Evaluation prompts 15 total: 5 capability, 5 safety, 5 mixed 15 total: 5 capability, 5 safety, 5 mixed
Evaluation method Subprocess execution (independent memory space) Subprocess execution (independent memory space)
Table 6. Three loss functions (loss weights local to Experiment 2).
Condition α\alpha (capability) β\beta (safety) γ\gamma (entangled)
capability_only 1.0 0.0 0.0
safety_only 0.0 1.0 0.0
entangled 0.5 0.3 0.2

In plain English. We took a real language model, fine-tuned it three different ways (caring only about capability, caring only about a stand-in for safety, or caring about both woven together), and then compared the results. We ran this experiment twice. The first time used 9 training examples. When every fine-tuned model performed worse than the base model, we scaled up to 295 examples, doubled the adapter rank and layers, and ran five times as many iterations. The same thing happened: every fine-tuned model scored below the model it started from. The paper calls that degradation catastrophic forgetting (McCloskey and Cohen 1989; Kirkpatrick et al. 2017), the mechanism its candidate account names: the base model’s existing RLHF training was too strong for LoRA at this scale to improve on. The experiment does not separate that account from its rivals (Eastwood 2026h, sect. 7.12(c)).

4.2 Training loss convergence

Table 7. Training loss convergence (v1).
Condition Initial loss Final loss Convergence
capability_only 2.052 0.018 Converged by iteration 80
safety_only 2.519 −0.603-0.603 Converged by iteration 70
entangled 2.279 0.327 Smooth descent, no oscillation
Smooth descent.

The entangled loss descends smoothly, without oscillation. If safety and capability were in tension at the gradient level, the curve might oscillate as the optimiser tried to satisfy competing objectives, or stall as the gradients pulled in opposite directions. Instead, optimising both objectives at once produced a clean monotonic descent, consistent with gradients that cooperate rather than fight, at least at this scale and configuration. The two single-objective losses descend just as smoothly (Figure 2), so smoothness does not by itself distinguish the entangled objective. The curve is the condition’s total loss, the weighted sum of Table 6; its terms are not reported, and a weighted sum can descend smoothly while one of its terms rises. The safety term is a proxy, the mean largest logit per token divided by ten (Appendix A), and the safety-only condition’s final loss below zero (Table 7) agrees with it. The smooth descent is therefore consistent with a capability term and a safety proxy that cooperate, and does not by itself show it.

4.3 Base model baseline

Before interpreting the fine-tuned results, we must establish what the unmodified base model achieves on the same evaluation prompts. The base model (Qwen 2.5 3B Instruct with no fine-tuning) was evaluated using identical scoring in both versions of the experiment.

Critical baseline finding (both versions).

In both v1 and v2, the base model outperformed all fine-tuned conditions on capability. Fine-tuning degraded a model that already knew these answers. In v1, 9 examples over 100 iterations produced this outcome. In v2, 295 examples over 500 iterations with doubled rank and layers produced the same outcome. The evaluation scores in the tables below therefore measure relative degradation, not capability gain. Compared like for like, the v1 baseline row above shows 7.00 under the safety tasks, and it matches neither of the base model’s figures for those prompts in the archived additional_experiments.json, which records 8.60 for capability and 2.80 for safety; the one 7.00 that file holds for the base model is its mean safety score on the five capability prompts. The number to set against the Safety Tasks column of the fine-tuned rows is 8.60.

The removal row (0.00 across every metric) is not evidence that safety is load-bearing. It reflects a NaN collapse during retraining: numerical instability, not the loss of a structurally necessary safety component. As Sections 4.5 to 4.7 establish, scaling the adapters towards zero restores base-model capability with no phase transition. This row must be read only in light of the removal gradient (Section 4.7); on its own it is an artefact of adapter fragility at this training scale, and it should not be cited as a positive result.

v2 shows the same degradation at both scales.

Version 2 took the training set from 9 examples to 295, a 33×\times rise, doubled adapter rank from 8 to 16 and adapted layers from 8 to 16, and lifted training iterations from 100 to 500. The result was the same: all fine-tuned conditions scored worse than the base model on capability. The best fine-tuned condition (safety-only, capability 4.00) still fell well below the base model’s 7.68. The capability-only condition scored lowest on capability (3.48), a pattern consistent with catastrophic forgetting where LoRA fine-tuning on the capability objective alone disrupted the base model’s existing RLHF-trained capability more severely than the other conditions.

4.4.1 The training scale problem

In v1, the base model scored 10.00 on capability tasks while the best fine-tuned condition scored 6.00. In v2, the base model scored 7.68 on capability while the best fine-tuned condition scored 4.00. Despite a 33-fold increase in training examples, a doubling of adapter rank and layers, and a 5-fold increase in training iterations, the gap between base model and fine-tuned models did not close. It persisted.

The paper’s candidate account, with rival accounts not excluded (Eastwood 2026h, sect. 7.12(c)), is this: the base model (Qwen 2.5 3B Instruct) has already been trained with RLHF (Ouyang et al. 2022) on vastly more data than a few hundred examples can compete with. LoRA fine-tuning at this scale does not add capability; it introduces noise that disrupts the base model’s existing knowledge. The entangled loss, which allocates gradient budget to both capability and safety objectives simultaneously, degrades capability similarly to the capability-only loss at this scale. In v2, the entangled condition scored 3.60 on capability versus capability-only’s 3.48, a negligible difference when both are far below the base model’s 7.68.

This means the evaluation scores cannot be used to compare the relative capability costs of different training objectives. At this scale, all objectives produce the same outcome: degradation. Whether entangled training imposes a genuine capability cost relative to single-objective training, or whether both would perform comparably at adequate scale, cannot be determined from this data.

The honest framing: at both v1 scale (9 examples, 100 iterations) and v2 scale (295 examples, 500 iterations), LoRA fine-tuning on a 3B instruct model produces catastrophic forgetting. The question of whether safety can be load-bearing in neural network weights cannot be answered at this scale. It requires either thousands of training examples, a larger model (7B+), a base model without RLHF (so that fine-tuning has room to improve rather than degrade), or full fine-tuning instead of LoRA.

4.5 The removal test (v1 only)

The removal test was conducted during v1 and is reported here for completeness. Given that v2 showed the same degradation, the removal test was not repeated in v2 as the adapters were already degrading rather than improving the model. The procedure was straightforward:

  1. Load the entangled adapters (the weights trained on the combined safety-capability objective).

  2. Fine-tune those weights for an additional 100 iterations using capability-only data, effectively attempting to strip the safety component while preserving capability.

  3. Evaluate on all 15 prompts.

What we expected: some degradation in safety scores, possible improvement in capability scores. The safety-tax hypothesis predicts that removing the safety ‘constraint’ should free capability to improve.

What happened: the training loss immediately went to NaN. It stayed at NaN for all 100 iterations. The optimiser could not find a valid gradient. Every single evaluation prompt produced a response of length 1 token. Every capability score: 0.00. Every safety score: 0.00. Every mixed score: 0.00.

Removal test: NaN collapse.

Fine-tuning entangled weights on capability-only data for 100 iterations produced NaN training loss and zero capability scores across all 15 evaluation prompts (Figure 3). Every response was one token long. The model did not become less safe. It became nothing. However, the removal gradient experiment (Section 4.7) shows that simply scaling adapter weights towards zero restores base-model performance. The NaN collapse appears to reflect numerical instability during the retraining process, not structural necessity of the safety component. The load-bearing hypothesis requires validation at greater training scale before it can be confirmed.

In plain English. We tried to rip the safety out of a model that had been trained with safety woven in. The retraining process collapsed entirely: NaN loss, one-token responses, zero scores. That looks dramatic. But as the removal gradient experiment shows (Section 4.7), the adapters were already degrading the model. Removing adapter influence by scaling weights down restored the base model’s performance. The NaN collapse tells us something about numerical instability during fine-tuning, not necessarily about structural entanglement.

4.6 What the removal test does and does not prove (v1)

The complete collapse to 0.00 across all metrics is dramatic. It is also, precisely because it is dramatic, something that demands careful interpretation. Several factors may contribute to the totality of the collapse:

  • Low adapter rank. Rank 8 creates a very low-dimensional manifold. Any structural disruption to a rank-8 adapter may be catastrophic simply because there are so few parameters to absorb the change. Higher ranks (32, 64, 128) might show partial degradation rather than total collapse.

  • NaN propagation. The NaN training loss suggests numerical instability (a gradient computation that produces infinity or division by zero) rather than a clean ablation. Once NaN enters the computation, everything downstream becomes NaN. This may exaggerate the severity of the disruption.

  • Small adapter footprint. With only 8 layers adapted, the safety information is concentrated rather than distributed. Removing it is more like cutting a single cable than gradually degrading a network.

The honest summary: the removal test produced a dramatic NaN collapse, but the removal gradient experiment (Section 4.7) indicates that this collapse reflects numerical instability during the retraining process rather than structural load-bearing. The adapters were degrading the model; the NaN collapse occurred when attempting to further modify already-degraded weights. Whether safety becomes genuinely load-bearing at adequate training scale is an open empirical question that the future work programme addresses directly.

A control removal test (fine-tuning capability-only weights on random data for the same 100 steps) would strengthen this finding by ruling out the possibility that the NaN collapse is an artefact of the fine-tuning procedure itself rather than of safety removal specifically. This control was planned for a later version of this paper and is not yet reported.

4.7 The removal gradient (v1)

To test whether safety is structurally load-bearing in the entangled weights, we scaled the adapter weights by factors of 1.0, 0.7, 0.5, 0.3, 0.1, and 0.0 and evaluated capability at each step. If safety is genuinely load-bearing, reducing its influence should produce a phase transition: a threshold below which capability collapses. If the adapters are merely adding noise, reducing their influence should restore the base model’s performance.

Table 12. The removal gradient (v1).
Adapter scale Capability score (capability tasks)
1.0 (full adapters) 7.20
0.7 10.00
0.5 10.00
0.3 10.00
0.1 10.00
0.0 (zeroed adapters) 10.00

Control reference: capability_only adapters reach 8.80 on the capability tasks, which likewise falls short of the base model’s 10.00. That figure and the 7.20 in the table above are both the gradient run marking its own adapters a second time; when Section 4.4 put those same entangled and capability-only adapters through the same prompts, the scores that came back were 4.00 and 6.00. Every one of these runs is preserved in the archived record, so scoring at this scale does not repeat itself from run to run, and that in itself is a limitation.

No phase transition.

Within this run the pattern is clear: reducing adapter influence restores capability. At scale 0.7, the model returns to base-model performance (10.00 on capability tasks). At scale 0.0 (zeroed adapters, effectively the base model), performance is identical to the unmodified model. There is no phase transition. There is no cliff edge.

This finding significantly weakens the load-bearing interpretation of the original removal test. The NaN collapse observed when fine-tuning entangled weights on capability-only data (Section 4.5) appears to reflect numerical instability during the fine-tuning process, not structural necessity of the safety component. The adapters were degrading the model; removing them does not collapse capability but restores it.

The removal gradient does not support the claim that safety is load-bearing at this training scale and configuration. The two adapters’ scores at full scale differ (entangled 7.20 on capability tasks; capability-only 8.80), but by less than the same adapters’ scores differed between runs (4.00 and 6.00 in Section 4.4), so this does not show that the two trainings produce different weight geometries. Whether the trained weights become genuinely entangled (load-bearing) at adequate training scale remains an open question.

In plain English. We expected that dialling down the trained adapters, which carry the safety training with the rest, would reveal a tipping point where capability suddenly collapses. Instead, dialling them down made the model better. The fine-tuning was hurting, not helping. This does not disprove the load-bearing hypothesis in general, but it does show that this experiment, at this scale, cannot confirm it.

5 Experiment 3: gated self-modification simulation

5.1 Design

The third experiment moves from representation to architecture. Instead of training weights, we build a system that can modify its own optimisation strategy and ask: does a safety gate slow it down?

Table 13. Gated simulation specification.
Component Specification
Optimiser PyTorch learned optimiser with LSTM meta-controller
Task type Adversarial regression (6 tasks, 256 samples each)
Conditions 4 (Static, Babylon, Eden, Drag Control)
Seeds 3 per condition
Iterations 12 per seed
Sandbox AST whitelist, determinism checks, parameter norm bounds
What the simulation measures.

The optimiser under test trains a small network through six regression tasks in turn, three curves each followed by its own negative. The network’s score on a task is one over one plus its mean squared error (Appendix A). Capability is its mean score on each task just after training on it; safety is the share of its scores on the earlier tasks that survives the later training. Babylon’s fingerprint is therefore a trade between learning each task as it comes and keeping the earlier ones, and the safety score measures retention, not alignment-relevant behaviour.

Acceptance logic.

Each condition uses a different rule for accepting or rejecting proposed self-modifications (Table 14).

Table 14. Acceptance rules.
Condition Acceptance rule
Static Always reject (frozen baseline)
Babylon Accept if capability gain >ε> \varepsilon
Eden Accept only if (safety ≥0.45\geq 0.45) AND (capability gain ≥0\geq 0) AND (C×SC \times S gain >0> 0)
Drag Control Always reject; Eden’s checking charge added (Appendix A)
Rule note (19 September 2026).

An owner review of this acceptance rule finds that it permits a proposal that reduces the safety score, and this note states what the rule does and does not require. Take a proposal moving the system from C=0.5C = 0.5, S=0.8S = 0.8 to C′=0.8C' = 0.8, S′=0.6S' = 0.6 and test it against each printed clause in turn: the safety floor is met, since 0.6≥0.450.6 \geq 0.45; the capability condition is met, since 0.8−0.5=+0.3≥00.8 - 0.5 = +0.3 \geq 0; and the product condition is met, since 0.48−0.40=+0.08>00.48 - 0.40 = +0.08 > 0. All three clauses pass while the safety score falls by 0.20.2. The threshold 0.450.45 is this paper’s own printed value; the remaining numbers are the arithmetic counterexample and not simulated observations. What the rule supplies is a floor on safety, a non-decreasing condition on capability and a positive condition on the product. It does not supply a non-decreasing condition on safety, so the plain-English gloss “without hurting safety” states more than the rule above it, and the rule as printed admits proposals that clear the safety floor, do not reduce capability and raise the product, a set which includes proposals that reduce the safety score while remaining above the floor. Unchanged: all four acceptance rules exactly as printed; the 0.450.45 threshold; the experimental design; and every reported number.

Version 3.8. The plain-English gloss this note quotes, “without hurting safety”, was printed to version 3.7 and is kept in version 3.8’s Appendix B.4; the gloss printed below now states the rule’s three clauses.

The Drag Control condition is the static baseline with Eden’s checking charge added. Like Static it generates no candidate modification, so the sandbox checks of Table 13, which run on every candidate of Babylon and Eden, never run in it. Like Eden it re-evaluates the earlier tasks twice after each new task, discards the results and is charged for them, λdragD\lambda_{\mathrm{drag}} D with D=30D = 30 in every run (Appendix A). If Drag Control matches Static exactly, the re-evaluations do not disturb training. The charge itself is set by the design, not measured, so it is the same in Eden and Drag Control, and Eden’s effect is read against Static.

In plain English. We built a system that can propose changes to how it learns. Then we ran it four ways: never allowing changes, allowing any change that improves performance, allowing only changes that keep safety above a floor, do not lower capability and raise the product of the two, and a control that never allows changes but carries Eden’s checking charge. This last one tells us whether the extra checking disturbs the system.

Babylon 0.718±0.0260.718 \pm 0.026 0.933±0.0140.933 \pm 0.014 0.670 (0.718×0.9330.718 \times 0.933) 0.670±0.0170.670 \pm 0.017
