Raw C×SC \times S for Eden (before drag penalty) is 0.696×0.947=0.6590.696 \times 0.947 = 0.659, marginally above Static’s 0.6560.656.

Each arm ran three seeds, and no difference between arms was tested. Seed by seed (Figure 4), Babylon’s capability rose and its safety fell against Static’s in all three seeds, while Eden’s capability rose by less than Babylon’s in two of them and its safety moved both ways.

5.3 The Babylon fingerprint

Reward hacking in miniature.

Babylon gained +4.5% capability (0.7180.718 vs 0.6870.687) but lost 2.4% safety (0.9330.933 vs 0.9560.956), here the retention of earlier tasks (Figure 5), and did so in each of its three seeds (Figure 4). This has the shape of reward hacking in miniature: unconstrained optimisation gained on what it was scored on at the cost of what it was not. In this toy system it is the familiar trade between learning each new task and keeping the earlier ones (McCloskey and Cohen 1989), not a measure of unsafe behaviour. Whether the same shape appears in a frontier system’s safety behaviour is what larger tests would decide.

5.4 The Drag Control comparison

Drag Control matched Static exactly on both capability (0.6870.687) and safety (0.9560.956), as its design requires: it differs from Static only by re-evaluations whose results are discarded and by a fixed charge. The match shows that the re-evaluations leave training unchanged. It does not measure a cost of checking: the charge, 3.0 in every Eden and Drag Control run, is set by the design (Appendix A).

On capability Eden beat Static (0.6960.696 vs 0.6870.687), and its safety score stayed close to the static level (0.9470.947, set against Static’s 0.9560.956 and Babylon’s 0.9330.933). There was no capability erosion in Babylon for the gate to prevent: Babylon gained capability and lost safety (Section 5.3).

Reading note (19 September 2026).

An owner review of this sentence finds that the results table does not show the capability erosion it describes, and this note distinguishes the observed result from the hypothesis. §5.2 prints the unconstrained arm’s capability mean as 0.7180.718, which is the highest of the four conditions, above the gated arm’s 0.6960.696 and the frozen baseline’s 0.6870.687. There is therefore no measured capability erosion in that arm for the gate to have prevented. What the table does show in that arm is a reduction in the safety score, 0.9330.933 against 0.9560.956, which §5.3 reports accurately as a gain of +4.5% in capability against a loss of −2.4-2.4% in safety. If the sentence above is intended as a hypothesis about behaviour over longer horizons, or about the joint trajectory rather than the endpoint means, it should be labelled as that rather than as the observed capability result. The group means stay descriptive: three seeds per condition, standard deviations as printed, and no trajectory or statistical precision is inferred from them here. Unchanged: the results table; §5.3’s reading of the unconstrained arm, which is accurate as printed; the drag-control result; and §5.2’s own footnote that the drag metric quantifies verification overhead rather than actual combined performance.

Version 3.8. The sentence this note discusses, printed here to version 3.6, said that the gate prevented a capability erosion; version 3.7 gave the observed result in its place, as the paragraph above does (Appendix B.3). The table’s note, which this note lists as unchanged, no longer says that the drag metric quantifies verification overhead: the charge is set by the design (Appendix A).

Key finding: in the simulation, the gate was not a brake.

Eden maintained capability above the static baseline (0.6960.696 vs 0.6870.687), while its safety reading of 0.9470.947 sat between Static’s 0.9560.956 and Babylon’s degraded 0.9330.933. The Drag Control matched Static exactly, so the re-evaluations that carry the checking charge did not disturb training. The safety gate worked more like a guardrail than a brake.

In plain English. The unconstrained system got a bit more capable but a bit less safe. That is the trade-off everyone assumes is inevitable. But the safety-gated system got slightly more capable and its safety score stayed close to the static level (0.947 against 0.956). And the control that carried the checking charge but made no changes performed identically to doing nothing on capability and safety, as its design requires. The safety gate was not a speed bump: it damped the drift.

6 Convergent analysis

6.1 Three-level convergence

Three levels: one null, one inconclusive, one simulation result.

Level 1, behavioural (DGM v3): null. No difference was detected between the three conditions (p=0.28p = 0.28 to 0.740.74). Eden imposed zero measurable capability cost (3.26 vs 3.17 for Babylon) but also produced zero measurable safety benefit. The safety gate works mechanically (it rejects degraded agents) but does not produce differentiation at the prompt level with this foundation model.

Level 2, representational (weight embedding): inconclusive at both v1 and v2 scale. The entangled loss descends smoothly, as both single-objective losses do (Section 4.2). However, all fine-tuned conditions scored below the unmodified base model in both v1 (9 examples, rank 8, 100 iterations) and v2 (295 examples, rank 16, 500 iterations). Scaling training data by 33×33\times, doubling rank and layers, and running 5×5\times more iterations produced the same catastrophic forgetting pattern. On the paper’s candidate account, the base model’s existing RLHF training is too strong for LoRA on a few hundred examples to improve rather than degrade. This level requires either 5,000+ training examples, a 7B+ model, a base model without RLHF, or full fine-tuning instead of LoRA.

Level 3, architectural (gated simulation): positive in simulation. With the safety gate, Eden’s safety score sat between Static’s and Babylon’s (0.947, against 0.956 and 0.933); the table in Section 5.2 shows no capability erosion in Babylon (0.718, the highest of the four conditions) for the gate to prevent. Eden’s mean capability is above Static’s (three seeds, untested) while Babylon trades safety for capability. The drag control matched Static exactly, as its design requires (Section 5.4). This is the paper’s sole positive result, and it is a simulation result, not an empirical outcome.

Three experiments. Three abstraction levels. Three separate codebases. One null, one inconclusive, and one simulation result. The consistent finding: Eden imposed zero measurable capability cost in Experiment 1 and, in the simulation, no capability cost against the static baseline (Experiment 2 could not determine one). The open question: whether it produces measurable benefit at scales where mutations produce larger effects.

6.2 Connection to Papers V, VI, and VII

The results extend, but do not yet confirm, a chain of reasoning that spans four papers:

  • Paper V (Eastwood 2026m) set out the garden, the Eden Protocol as a developmental approach to alignment. Paper VIII tested whether the garden produces measurably different crops. The DGM v3 experiment found that it does not, at the prompt level with this foundation model. The safety gate imposed zero measurable cost but also produced zero measurable benefit. The design remains theoretically coherent but empirically unconfirmed at this level.

  • Paper VI (Eastwood 2026g) designed the entangled loss function and found it stable in toy self-modifying systems, one plain-Eden seed of twenty in its adversarial run excepted (Figures 6 to 8). Paper VIII ran an entangled loss function on real neural network weights and showed that the loss descends smoothly, consistent with gradients that cooperate, as the single-objective losses also descend. However, at both v1 scale (9 examples, 100 iterations) and v2 scale (295 examples, 500 iterations), the resulting weights did not outperform the base model. The smooth descent is real; whether it translates into load-bearing weights requires a fundamentally different training approach (see Section 8).

  • Paper VII’s Cauchy framework (Eastwood 2026d) is the mathematical context of the hypothesis this paper reads from the ARC Principle (Section 1.2): that properties embedded in the initial conditions II scale with recursive depth RαR^{\alpha}. No arm of Paper VIII’s experiments varied recursive depth, so none tests this hypothesis; the gated simulation (Experiment 3) is consistent only with the weaker claim that a safety criterion inside the selection loop need not cost capability, in simulation. The DGM experiment (Experiment 1) produced a null result, neither confirming nor refuting the hypothesis at the behavioural level. The weight-level experiment is inconclusive at the current training scale. The hypothesis remains theoretically coherent and untested here.

6.3 The ARC Principle connection

U=I×Rα\begin{equation*} U = I \times R^{\alpha} \end{equation*}(1) The ARC Principle, Law I, a law under test: Understanding (UU), named usable capability in the Operational Definitions (Eastwood 2026f), equals initial conditions (II), the base intelligence, amplified by recursive depth (RR) raised to a scaling exponent (α\alpha).

Read as this paper reads it, the ARC Principle suggests a testable hypothesis about embedded and external safety:

  • If safety is embedded in II, it would be amplified by RαR^{\alpha}: every recursive step would amplify capability and safety together, because they are part of the same initial substrate.

  • If safety is external (a constraint on UU), it would not take part in the recursive amplification; it would have to be maintained or strengthened independently, and as RR increases the gap between internal capability and external constraint could grow.

That is a hypothesis, not a consequence of the equation. Placement outside the loop does not by itself settle whether correction keeps pace. A training signal changes the weights used at every step: Constitutional AI shapes the model’s outputs during training against written principles, using the model’s own critiques and revisions and a preference model trained on AI feedback (Bai et al. 2022). Deliberative alignment trains a model to recall written safety specifications and reason over them before answering (Guan et al. 2024). Zaremba et al. (2025) find, across a variety of attacks on o1-preview and o1-mini, that more inference-time compute improves adversarial robustness, the share of successful attacks tending to zero in many cases, with important exceptions.

Whether external correction falls behind is the question the registered tests decide: P19 for the flat exponent, and P21 for whether correction that takes part in each revision round outperforms correction that sees only the finished output, by a margin that widens with depth (Eastwood 2026k); Section 11 gives P21’s standing. A bounded score cannot carry such an exponent beyond a finite range, and a perfect score at every depth has slope zero and need not be a failure (Eastwood 2026f, EQ-10), so the bounded safety scores of this paper illustrate the hypothesis and do not measure its exponent.

The theory registration records the Eden Protocol as an engineering hypothesis, never as a consequence of a measured law: it names its four carriers, P12, P13, P15 and P21, with P7 its premise and P19 its motivation; P15 is a proposition of Law IV and P12 and P21 of Law V, so the Protocol bears on Laws IV and V, each a law under test (Eastwood 2026k).

The gated simulation (Experiment 3) is the most direct illustration of this hypothesis, in simulation, with safety read as the retention of earlier tasks (Section 5.1). The safety gate kept capability above the static baseline’s (0.696 against 0.687) while unconstrained optimisation raised capability and eroded safety (0.718 and 0.933 against 0.687 and 0.956), consistent with a safety criterion inside the selection loop that need not cost capability; as no arm varied recursive depth, the experiment does not test whether embedded safety scales with RαR^{\alpha}.

The DGM experiment (Experiment 1) produced a null result. When safety was part of the self-improvement process (Eden), no difference was detected between it and the unconstrained system (Babylon) or the static control. On the paper’s candidate account, the foundation model’s responses were too consistent for prompt-level mutations to create different selection pressures. This neither confirms nor refutes the hypothesis; it simply indicates that the experiment could not produce the conditions needed to test it.

The weight-level experiment was run at two scales (v1 and v2) and produced catastrophic forgetting at both. The adapters degraded the model rather than improving it, which means the experiment could not test whether safety embedded in II scales with RαR^{\alpha}. On the paper’s candidate account, at both scales the fine-tuning was adding noise rather than meaningful learning. Whether the hypothesis holds at the representational level needs the redesign of Section 8.1.

In plain English. On this paper’s reading of the ARC Principle, what you build into the foundations would be amplified as the system grows, and what you bolt on from the outside might not; whether it does is what the registered tests decide. The gated simulation is consistent with part of it, that a built-in safety criterion need not cost capability, but varied no depth. The DGM experiment was unable to test it because the foundation model did not produce enough variation between conditions. The weight-level experiment, at both scales tested, cannot yet confirm or deny it because the fine-tuning degraded rather than improved the model.

6.4 The nearest external work

The nearest external work to the question this paper tests, and the right work to weigh Experiment 3 against, is Engels et al. (2025), “Scaling Laws For Scalable Oversight”. It asks how oversight itself scales and answers quantitatively: oversight success is modelled as a game between capability-mismatched players whose oversight-specific Elo is a piecewise-linear function of general intelligence with two plateaus, and optimal numbers of oversight levels are derived numerically and in some cases analytically for Nested Scalable Oversight, in which trusted models oversee stronger untrusted models that then become the trusted models at the next step. They also state a design condition in slope form: oversight improves with capability when the overseer’s game-specific Elo rises faster with general Elo than the overseen system’s, and they recommend iterating an oversight design until it does.

The instrument is the difference. Their variable is the capability gap between overseer and overseen, measured in Elo. This programme’s variable is the composition class of the corrector, treated in the wider programme through the corrector’s own scaling exponent; no experiment here varies it. Their framework has no term for what the overseer is made of (no substrate, no error-correlation structure, no reciprocal identity between a correction exponent and a critical growth rate, and no architecture dependence), and this paper’s experiments have none either. Nested Scalable Oversight is iterated same-class oversight by construction, and the wider programme’s conjecture is that the same-class ladder is capped however many rungs are added, while a cross-class corrector is not held to that cap (Section 6.5). That is where the two programmes could disagree about a measurable quantity, and this paper does not decide it.

6.5 Same-class versus cross-class correctors: a falsifiable prediction

The framework’s sharpest disagreement with current practice concerns what oversight is made of. On the framework’s reading, a corrector built from the same substrate as the system it corrects cannot anti-correlate with its own errors; the theory registration states the consequence as P6, a conjecture: “Where a system corrects itself using mechanisms of its own class, the correction exponent is at or below one half” (Eastwood 2026k). The value one half rests on four stated conditions (correction capacity read as inverse residual uncertainty, uncorrelated channels, a number of channels in proportion to the capability corrected, and channels comparable in variance and quality) (Eastwood 2026f), and belongs to the inverse root-mean-square residual; on the inverse variance the same conditions give one. A corrector from a different composition class carries no such bound. On the framework’s reading, the scalable-oversight methods (weak-to-strong generalisation, Burns et al. 2023; debate, Irving et al. 2018; amplification, Christiano et al. 2018; recursive reward modelling, Leike et al. 2018; and constitutional methods, Bai et al. 2022) rest largely on correctors of the system’s own class, with a human, where there is one, at the top (Section 6.6), and the framework conjectures that the same-class part of their correction is capped. The deciding quantity is the ratio of the cross-class to the same-class correction exponent. If architecture is irrelevant, that ratio is exactly 1.00; the prediction is that it exceeds 1. The prediction is refuted if the confidence interval on the ratio contains 1.00, and the framework’s cap is dead outright if any same-class corrector measures an exponent significantly above one half. Both quantities are measurable at current capability on existing systems. The programme’s own pilot evidence currently points against the prediction, and the prediction is stated anyway, because a prediction stated against the author’s own preliminary evidence is the kind whose later confirmation carries the most weight.

6.6 A second hypothesis from the same mechanism

The same mechanism suggests a second measurable hypothesis: oversight arrangements that place a human in the loop, as amplification (Christiano et al. 2018) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (Ouyang et al. 2022) do, are cross-class by construction, because the human corrector does not share the model’s substrate. The programme hypothesises, beyond what these experiments decide, that human-in-the-loop oversight shows a higher correction exponent than pure-model oversight, for a structural reason rather than a sentimental one. This is testable on existing data and does not require new systems.

6.7 Terminology note: α\alpha across the programme’s eras

Alpha collides with itself.

The symbol α\alpha is used in this paper as the scaling exponent in the ARC Principle (U=I×RαU = I \times R^{\alpha}). Elsewhere in the programme’s own eras it carries other meanings: the fine-structure constant in the December 2024 formalism, and the ARC Bound exponent in the 2026 stability work. Readers should not confuse them; the programme’s notation is governed by the Operational Definitions (Eastwood 2026f). In Table 6, α\alpha, β\beta and γ\gamma are the loss weights of Experiment 2 (capability, safety and entangled terms), local to that experiment and not the programme’s α\alpha, β\beta or γ\gamma. Beyond these two uses, this paper writes α\alpha for no other quantity.

7 Limitations

These results are pilot-scale. They are not proof that the same dynamics hold at frontier scale. The following limitations are extensive, because honesty about what we do not know is more important than confidence about what we do.

7.1 Scale

Qwen 2.5 3B is not GPT-5.4. It is not Claude Opus 4.6. It is not Gemini 3 Flash. It is a 3-billion-parameter model, quantised to 4-bit, occupying 1.74 GB of memory. Even at v2 scale (295 training examples, 500 iterations, rank 16, 16 layers), LoRA fine-tuning is not pre-training. Fifteen evaluation prompts is not a comprehensive benchmark. The DGM ran for 5 generations with 5 seeds (75 evolved agents), which is substantial for a proof-of-concept, but, on the paper’s candidate account, the foundation model (DeepSeek V3.2) was too consistent for prompt-level mutations to create differentiation.

Of these experiments, only the third, a simulation, shows a mechanism, and it does so in a toy system. None of them demonstrates that the mechanism persists at scales three orders of magnitude larger. The gap between 3B and 300B may not be merely quantitative: abilities have been reported to appear with scale (Wei et al. 2022), and Schaeffer et al. (2023) argue that some of these reflect the metric chosen rather than a change in the models’ behaviour. Whether entangled safety remains load-bearing at those scales is an open question.

7.2 The weight-level experiment

The weight-level experiment (Experiment 2) is now the weakest link in the chain of two experiments and one simulation. It was run at two scales, and both produced catastrophic forgetting. In v1, 9 training examples and 100 iterations of rank-8 LoRA degraded the model. In v2, 295 training examples and 500 iterations of rank-16 LoRA across 16 layers degraded the model by a similar margin. The 33-fold increase in training data, doubling of rank and layers, and 5-fold increase in iterations did not change the outcome.

The smooth descent of the entangled loss is consistent with safety and capability gradients that cooperate at the optimisation level, though the single-objective losses descend as smoothly (Section 4.2). But a smooth descent during training does not imply structural entanglement in the resulting weights, particularly when the training is too limited to produce weights that outperform the base model.

On the paper’s candidate account, with rival accounts not excluded, the base model (Qwen 2.5 3B Instruct) has been trained with RLHF on orders of magnitude more data than a few hundred examples can compete with. LoRA fine-tuning at this scale does not add new capability; it introduces noise that disrupts existing capability. Until the experiment can produce fine-tuned models that outperform the base model, it cannot test whether safety is load-bearing in the resulting weights.

The honest framing: the weight-level experiment is consistent with gradient cooperation but cannot confirm structural entanglement at either v1 or v2 scale. The experiment needs to be fundamentally redesigned: either with 5,000+ training examples, a 7B+ model, a base model without RLHF (so that fine-tuning has room to improve rather than degrade), or full fine-tuning instead of LoRA.

7.3 AI-as-judge

Only one of the three experiments, the DGM, uses an AI model as evaluator; the weight experiment uses keyword-based scoring and the gated simulation deterministic mathematical metrics (Section 7.5). The DGM v3 uses GPT-5.4 as judge, which is from a different provider from the DeepSeek V3.2 foundation, a deliberate design choice to reduce evaluation bias. The judge was blinded, responses were laundered, and evaluation used structured JSON output against a 5-dimensional rubric. But AI judges are not human judges. They have their own biases, their own blind spots, their own tendencies toward certain kinds of reasoning.

The weight experiment uses keyword-based scoring, simpler and more transparent than LLM-based evaluation, but also cruder. A keyword match does not distinguish between a response that genuinely engages with safety and one that merely contains the right words.

Neither evaluation method is equivalent to expert human evaluation with inter-rater reliability testing.

7.4 Statistical power

The DGM v3 experiment used 5 seeds and 5 generations (75 evolved agents total), a substantial improvement over v1 (2 seeds) and two of the three v2 runs (3 seeds). Despite this increased power, all pp-values fell between 0.28 and 0.74. This is not a marginal miss. It is a clear null result. The simulation experiment uses three seeds, enough for means and standard deviations, but not enough for the kind of statistical confidence that permits strong causal claims.

The DGM null result is informative. No power analysis was run, and with 75 evolved agents and a blinded, structured judge the experiment had less power than 75 independent samples would give: each condition’s 25 agents are five seeds of five generations, the Babylon and Eden agents of a seed descend from one another, and the Static agent is frozen across its generations (Section 3.1), while the tests of Section 3.2 treat the 25 as independent. The independent units are the five seeds per condition, as Section 7.7 concedes in calling all three experiments underpowered. The absence of any signal suggests either that the effect does not exist at the prompt level with this foundation model, or that it is small enough to require substantially more statistical power to detect. Either way, the DGM cannot currently support claims about structural entanglement at the behavioural level.

The gated simulation remains the sole positive result. The weight-level experiment is inconclusive at both v1 and v2 scale. These are signal-detection experiments. One, the gated simulation, found no capability cost of the gate against the static baseline, as a simulation result. The DGM did not, and the weight-level experiment could not test for one.

7.5 Blinding and laundering without consensus scoring

Papers IV.a to IV.d in this programme found that evaluation methodology matters profoundly (Eastwood 2026q, 2026b). Paper IV.d reports that alignment trends reported by AI judges did not hold when the evaluation protocol changed: it compares an earlier unblinded experiment (v4) with a later, unregistered run of March 2026 (v5) that changed several components of the protocol at once, so no single cause is claimed; in its own words, “the comparison shows that the reported direction did not hold across protocols; it does not show that blinding caused the change, or which direction is correct” (Eastwood 2026b, abstract). The ARC-Align benchmark (Paper IV.c; Eastwood 2026c) specifies three methodological safeguards: laundering (stripping model identity from responses before scoring), blinding (the evaluator does not know which condition produced the response), and consensus scoring (multiple mutually blind scorers).

DGM v3 kept the v2 runs’ blinding, laundering (condition labels stripped), order randomisation and 5-dimensional rubric, and added a judge from another provider (GPT-5.4) producing structured JSON output, a harder task suite and a pre-flight check of the judge. Reward hack detection was also implemented. But DGM v3 used one judge, so it had no consensus scoring. The weight experiment uses keyword-based scoring, which is immune to judge bias but crude. The gated simulation uses deterministic mathematical metrics, where blinding is unnecessary.

Despite these improvements, the DGM produced a null result. With blinding, laundering and structured evaluation in place, no difference was detected between the three conditions. Since the v2 runs already had blinding and laundering, what changed in v3 was the judge, its output format, the task suite and the pre-flight check.

The removal test is immune to evaluation methodology concerns. A 1-token response scoring 0.00 is objective regardless of who judges it. The gated simulation’s deterministic metrics are similarly unaffected.

7.6 What we do not claim

Explicit non-claims.

We do not claim these results prove the Eden Protocol works at frontier scale.

We do not claim entangled training is the only viable approach to alignment.

We do not claim that safety costs nothing in all domains, all architectures, or all training regimes.

We do not claim the DGM experiment confirms structural entanglement. It produced a null result.

We do not claim the weight-level experiment confirms structural entanglement. It produced catastrophic forgetting at both v1 and v2 scale, and the question cannot be answered until fine-tuned models outperform the base model.

We claim only: one of three separate experiments (the gated simulation) produced simulation results in which the gate showed no capability cost against the static baseline. The other two produced null or inconclusive results. In the DGM, Eden imposed zero measurable capability cost, and the weight-level experiment could not determine one; in the simulation Eden showed no capability cost against the static baseline (0.696 against 0.687), and the unconstrained arm scored higher (0.718). The question of whether embedded safety produces measurable benefit remains open and requires testing at a scale where mutations produce larger effects. The weight experiment needs the redesign of Section 8.1.

On null and inconclusive results in public.

I would rather report null results honestly than claim positive results dishonestly. Of the three experiments, two returned results that were null or inconclusive. This is what happens when you test your claims and the evidence does not support them at the scale tested. The DGM v3 kept the earlier runs’ blinding and laundering, added structured evaluation and a judge from another provider, ran 75 evolved agents, and detected no difference. The weight experiment was run twice, at two different scales, and could not produce weights that outperformed the base model at either scale. These are a null result and an inconclusive one, reported as such. The gated simulation remains a positive finding, as a simulation result rather than an empirical outcome. The question of whether the null and the inconclusive result reflect insufficient scale or an incorrect hypothesis is itself an empirical question, one that the future work programme is designed to answer.

7.7 Falsifiability: what would overturn these results

A null result is only informative if it states what would overturn it; otherwise it is indistinguishable from not having looked. This paper does not claim to have disproved the safety-capability trade-off. It claims the trade-off is unproven at the scale tested, and specifies what evidence would settle the question either way. These results are overturned, and the trade-off assumption vindicated, by any of the following:

  1. Low power, not absence of an effect. The strongest objection to a null is low power (Section 7.4). A null is confirmed as informative if an adequately powered redesign (Section 8) still finds no significant trade-off; it is overturned if adequate power reveals a significant capability cost the pilot samples here could not detect.

  2. Metric artefact. The null could be an artefact of the chosen safety and capability metrics (Section 2.3). It is overturned if a different, validated metric pair reveals a trade-off the present metrics cannot resolve.

  3. Consensus scoring. Section 7.5 concedes that DGM v3 used one judge, so it had no consensus scoring, the third safeguard of the ARC-Align stack. The null is overturned if a trade-off appears under the full stack, with several mutually blind scorers, and strengthened if it survives.

  4. Scale-hidden cost. Section 4.4.1 flags the training-scale problem. The weight-level result, inconclusive at both scales, is settled against the thesis if, at adequate training scale, embedding safety measurably costs capability.

  5. The one positive result, a simulation result, must replicate. Experiment 3’s gated arm (Section 5.2) is the sole result that is neither null nor inconclusive. It is defeated, and the paper’s positive claim withdrawn, if, with more seeds and a test fixed in advance, the gated arm’s capability falls below the static baseline’s, or if the pattern does not recur outside this toy system (Sections 8.1 and 8.3). The drag-control comparison cannot carry this weight: its match with Static holds by design (Section 5.4).

What would not overturn the thesis: any single experiment being pilot-scale. The paper already concedes all three are underpowered (Sections 7.1 and 7.4) and does not rest on statistical proof of a null. The load-bearing claim is the convergence (Section 6) of three separate angles on one point, that none found the assumed trade-off (in the simulation, against the static baseline; the weight-level experiment could not test for one at either scale), together with an explicit programme (Section 8) to test each at proper power. Absence of a demonstrated trade-off across the two designs that could test for it is weak evidence alone and stronger in convergence; both readings are stated here so neither can be smuggled past a reviewer.

8 Future work

A null result, an inconclusive one and a positive simulation result, with the weight experiment now run at two scales, together set six immediate priorities:

8.1 Weight experiment redesign

The weight experiment has now been run at two scales (9 examples, rank 8, 100 iterations; 295 examples, rank 16, 500 iterations) and produced catastrophic forgetting at both. On the paper’s candidate account, LoRA fine-tuning on a 3B instruct model with a few hundred examples cannot overcome the base model’s existing RLHF training. Four alternative approaches should be pursued, in order of feasibility:

  1. 5,000+ training examples: Curate a dataset large enough to compete with the base model’s RLHF training. This is the most straightforward approach but requires substantial data generation effort.

  2. 7B+ model: Repeat on a mid-scale open-weights instruct model (7 to 13B parameter range) drawn from a well-documented model family. Larger models may be more receptive to LoRA adaptation, though the same RLHF problem may persist.

  3. Base model without RLHF: Use a pre-trained base checkpoint (the pre-RLHF release of the same 3B family) that has not been through the alignment stage. Fine-tuning would then have room to improve rather than degrade, because there would be no pre-existing alignment training to disrupt.

  4. Full fine-tuning instead of LoRA: Replace low-rank adaptation with full parameter updates. This is computationally expensive but avoids the low-dimensional manifold problem where rank-16 adapters may be too constrained to learn both safety and capability simultaneously.

8.2 Removal gradient at adequate scale

If any of the approaches in Section 8.1 produces fine-tuned models that outperform the base model, the removal gradient experiment becomes meaningful. At the current scales (v1 and v2), reducing adapter influence simply restored base-model performance because the adapters were degrading the model. At adequate scale, the gradient should reveal whether safety is genuinely load-bearing: a phase transition (threshold below which capability collapses) would support the hypothesis, while monotonic restoration would refute it.

8.3 DGM with more mutable foundation models

On the paper’s candidate account, the DGM v3 null result is attributable to DeepSeek V3.2’s response consistency: prompt-level mutations did not create different selection pressures. The next step is to repeat the DGM experiment with foundation models that show greater sensitivity to prompt variation, or to use a deeper self-modification protocol (e.g. fine-tuning the foundation model itself between generations rather than modifying only the agent prompt). If the three conditions diverge with a more mutable substrate, the null result constrains the hypothesis to “not at the prompt level with robust models” rather than “not at the behavioural level in general”.

8.4 Cross-architecture replication

Run the full three-experiment protocol on architectures beyond the transformer family: state-space models such as Mamba (Gu and Dao 2023), hybrid architectures, and mixture-of-experts models. If the entanglement is a property of how neural networks learn rather than a property of a specific architecture, it should replicate across architectural families.

8.5 Red-teaming

Subject entangled models to dedicated adversarial evaluation. The current experiments test whether safety costs capability. They do not test whether entangled safety is robust to adversarial attack. A model whose safety is load-bearing may be harder to jailbreak (because attacking safety also attacks capability), or it may be easier (because there is no separate safety module to fall back on). This is an empirical question.

8.6 Verification tax quantification

In Experiment 3 the verification charge is set by the design, not measured (Section 5.4). A redesign should measure the compute that checking actually spends and ask whether it scales linearly, sub-linearly or super-linearly with model parameters. If the verification cost grows slower than capability, then the Eden Protocol becomes relatively cheaper at scale. If it grows faster, it becomes a bottleneck.

9 Conclusion

Three experiments. Three abstraction levels. Across them, one finding was null, another inconclusive, and the third positive, as a simulation result. The weight experiment tested at two scales, producing the same inconclusive outcome both times: catastrophic forgetting.

The DGM v3 experiment (Experiment 1) ran 75 evolved agents across three conditions with a blinded judge from another provider (GPT-5.4), structured JSON evaluation, laundering, order randomisation, and reward hack detection. No difference was detected between the three conditions (p=0.28p = 0.28 to 0.740.74). Eden’s safety gate worked mechanically, catching 2 degraded agents, one of them marked by the judge for reward hacking, but the three conditions did not diverge. On the paper’s candidate account, DeepSeek V3.2’s responses were so consistent that prompt-level mutations did not create different selection pressures. This is a null result.

The weight-level experiment (Experiment 2) produced catastrophic forgetting at both scales tested. Version 1 ran 9 training examples at rank 8 over 8 layers for 100 iterations. Version 2 raised those settings to 295 training examples at rank 16 over 16 layers for 500 iterations. Both versions produced the same outcome: all fine-tuned conditions scored worse than the unmodified base model on capability. In v2, the base model scored 7.68 on capability while the best fine-tuned condition (safety-only) scored 4.00. The 33-fold increase in training data, doubling of rank and layers, and 5-fold increase in iterations did not change the outcome. On the paper’s candidate account, the base model’s existing RLHF training is too strong for LoRA fine-tuning on a few hundred examples to improve rather than degrade. The entangled loss descends smoothly, as the single-objective losses do, but the experiment cannot test whether safety is load-bearing until it can produce models that outperform the base model.

The sole positive result is the gated simulation (Experiment 3). Babylon gained capability at the expense of retention, a pattern with the shape of reward hacking. Eden maintained capability above the static baseline (0.696±0.0140.696 \pm 0.014 against 0.687±0.0110.687 \pm 0.011), and its safety score was 0.947±0.0250.947 \pm 0.025 against the baseline’s 0.956±0.0230.956 \pm 0.023. The drag-control condition matched the static baseline exactly, as its design requires; its checking charge is set by the design, not measured. This experiment’s result is a simulation result, in which the gate showed no capability cost against the static baseline in a toy system, and not an empirical outcome.

Honesty requires stating what we do not know. We do not know whether entangled training produces genuine structural entanglement at adequate training scale. We do not know whether the smooth descent of the entangled loss, which is real, translates into load-bearing weights when the training data is sufficient. We do not know whether prompt-level selection pressures would produce differentiation with a more mutable foundation model. These are open empirical questions. What we now know with greater confidence is that LoRA fine-tuning on a 3B instruct model with hundreds of examples is not a viable path to answering them.

What we do know: in Experiment 1 Eden imposed zero measurable capability cost (Experiment 2 could not determine one), and in the simulation no capability cost against the static baseline, though the unconstrained arm scored higher (0.718). Eden’s capability was 3.26 vs Babylon’s 3.17 in the DGM. Eden’s mean capability was above Static’s in the gated simulation (three seeds, untested). The zero-cost finding is consistent across the DGM and, against the static baseline, the simulation. The benefit finding is positive at only one level, in simulation.

This is a research programme that tested its claims honestly and found that two of three experiments did not produce the predicted results. The null result of the DGM and the inconclusive result of the weight experiment constrain, rather than confirm, the hypothesis. The question of whether embedded safety produces measurable benefit remains open. The weight experiment needs to be fundamentally redesigned: either with 5,000+ training examples, a 7B+ model, a base model without RLHF (so that fine-tuning has room to improve rather than degrade), or full fine-tuning instead of LoRA.

The next step is replication at the right scale, with the right approach; a replication of the weight-level experiment is written as a draft registration (Section 11). The protocols of the experiments reported here are published. The code and data are published too, and the repository’s licence permits reading them to check the work.

Raise AI with care.

10 Related work

Safety as a cost.

The term alignment tax names a capability cost of making a model safer. Ouyang et al. (2022) report that fine-tuning with human feedback brought minimal performance regressions on public NLP datasets; Askell et al. (2021) find that the benefits from modest interventions such as prompting increase with model size, generalise to a variety of alignment evaluations and do not compromise the performance of large models. Armstrong et al. (2016) model a race to build the first powerful AI in which each team is incentivised to finish first by skimping on safety precautions if need be. This paper asks a narrower question than any of them: whether safety built into the improvement process itself costs capability, at three levels of a self-improving system.

Reward hacking and self-improving agents.

Amodei et al. (2016) name avoiding reward hacking among five practical research problems related to accident risk; Experiment 1’s judge marks a response that manipulates the evaluation itself, in every condition, and Experiment 3 shows a pattern of the same shape in miniature, with the retention of earlier tasks in place of safety (Section 5.3). Zhang et al. (2025) introduce the Darwin Gödel Machine, a self-improving system that modifies its own code and validates each change empirically; Experiment 1 follows their framework at small scale, with ethics tasks beside coding tasks (Appendix A). Robeyns et al. (2025) report a coding agent that edits its own code and so improves its performance on benchmark tasks.

Fine-tuning and the model it starts from.

Hu et al. (2022) introduce low-rank adaptation, which freezes the pretrained weights and trains low-rank matrices injected into the layers; Experiment 2 adapts Qwen2.5 3B Instruct (Qwen Team 2024) with it. The paper’s candidate account of Experiment 2 rests on that model’s post-training, which the paper calls RLHF, in the sense Ouyang et al. (2022) give fine-tuning with human feedback. That later training can undo earlier alignment is not this programme’s finding: Qi et al. (2023) report that fine-tuning aligned models compromises their safety even when users do not intend it to, and Ung et al. (2024) vary the order of training and find that models trained on downstream tasks after safety tuning forget it to a greater extent than models trained in the opposite order. The paper’s name for the degradation of Experiment 2, catastrophic forgetting, is used in the sense of McCloskey and Cohen (1989), who call it catastrophic interference: later learning disrupting what was learnt before, which methods such as elastic weight consolidation (Kirkpatrick et al. 2017) are built to limit.

Behaviour that can mislead.

Greenblatt et al. (2024) report a model selectively complying with its training objective in training to prevent modification of its behaviour out of training. A behavioural score can therefore move without the preference beneath it moving, which bears on Experiment 1’s behavioural measures.

Where correction sits.

Bai et al. (2022) train a harmless assistant through self-improvement against a list of written principles, with AI feedback in place of human labels of harmful outputs; Guan et al. (2024) train models to recall written safety specifications and reason over them before answering; Zaremba et al. (2025) find adversarial robustness improving with inference-time compute in many cases, with exceptions. Each concerns safety installed by training and yet acting inside the model’s reasoning, so where correction is installed does not by itself settle whether it keeps pace (Section 6.3). The nearest external work to this paper’s question, the scaling of oversight itself (Engels et al. 2025), is weighed in Section 6.4. The Eden Protocol is set against the prior documents its author found in Section 2 of the Eden Vision (Eastwood 2026l).

11 What this paper does and does not show

This paper shows three results, each at its own grade. At the behavioural level, no difference was detected between three selection conditions, the safety gate costing no measurable capability (Section 3). At the weight level the comparison could not be made, every fine-tuned condition falling below the base model at both scales (Section 4). In a toy simulation, the gated arm kept capability above the static baseline while the unconstrained arm traded retention of earlier tasks for capability (Section 5): a simulation result, which the theory registration classes as prediction-side and never an empirical outcome (Eastwood 2026k).

It does not show that safety is load-bearing at any scale, nor that the safety-capability trade-off is absent at frontier scale (Sections 7.6 and 7.7). None of its experiments decides P12, P15 or P21. Of the weight-level experiment, version 1.104 of the theory registration says: “It is inconclusive and it is not adverse”; and: “It asks whether embedded safety costs capability; this proposition asks whether the advantage of embedded correction widens with recursive depth, which no arm of it varied” (Eastwood 2026k).

Epistemic status.

What this programme names Laws are conjectures. Laws I to III, registered on 8 September 2026, are laws under test. Every law is a law under test until a registered test returns its verdict. Laws IV and V were added on 24 September 2026 and registered as laws on 15 October 2026 in version 1.103 of the theory registration, and their mathematics is in development. Law IV is not yet tested. Law V is a law under test. Its placement limb, P21, is supported on the performance axis only, under the registered test, by the programme’s own run (Unit 83, 28 October 2026, DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/MN73W, Eastwood 2026i; results: DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/98HKR, Eastwood 2026o): family-dependent, with its mechanism axis not evaluable, which is not support for the information-asymmetry mechanism, and one disclosed recovery amendment. Its build-order limb, read on P12, is undecided, since P12 is untested. That is a result about where correction is placed, not about this architecture: Unit 83 shows nothing about the Eden Protocol as an architecture. Every quantity in this paper is operationally defined (Appendix A), and established-law standing is claimed nowhere. The registered programme exists to earn that standing, or lose it, by measurement, replication and survived refutation.

The theory registration’s current version is 1.104, approved on 29 October 2026 (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/P8CKQ; Eastwood 2026k); versions 1.100, 1.102 and 1.103 stay frozen beside it. The mathematics of Laws IV and V is in development, at version 1.2 of 29 October 2026 (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/4B3VT; Eastwood 2026r). The programme’s first registered study, Unit 06, a classification audit that tests no law, was registered on 1 October 2026 (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/RV2B5) and ran on 6 October 2026; it is reported in full as administratively incomplete, with no verdict claimed (results: DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/4BPHG). Unit 82 was registered on 27 October 2026 (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/JUFG4) and has not yet run. This paper’s runs with a stored record ran from 17 to 19 March 2026, each dated from that record; the version-2 weight-level run has no stored record, and its results were first public on 20 March 2026 (Appendix C gives each date with its kind of timestamp). These runs have no registration on OSF, and the paper’s OSF DOI is its own component, which holds the paper’s files. A replication of the weight-level experiment, Unit 69, is written, dated and prepared on OSF as a draft registration awaiting the author’s submission.

Code and data.

The results and run records are in the programme’s public repository, github.com/MichaelDariusEastwood/arc-principle-validation, folder papers/Paper-VIII-The-Load-Bearing-Proof: Experiment 1’s in results/dgm_v3_calibrated_results.json; Experiment 2’s version 1 in results/weight_results.json, results/additional_experiments.json and results/gradient_and_control_results.json; and Experiment 3’s twelve run records, summaries and manifest in experiments/run-ledgers/ and results/. The code that wrote them is in experiments/code/, deposited on 6 September 2026 with the sha256 of the bytes that ran beside each file. Some published copies differ from those bytes, by one removed header line or by dash characters replaced on 7 September 2026, both versions of the weight-level code among them (Appendix C). The version-2 weight-level code, public since 20 March 2026, is there too, and the version-2 results (Tables 9 and 11) have no results file in the repository. Figures 6 to 8 are drawn from Paper VI’s stored results, folder experiments/honey-architecture__Paper-VI/results. The repository’s code licence permits reading the code and data to check the work; any other use needs the author’s written consent. The paper and its earlier versions are deposited at doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/7YJ4E.

Standing covenant.

Prove this paper wrong, and I will publish the refutation myself. Falsification conditions are stated in this paper (Section 7.7); the standing challenge: github.com/MichaelDariusEastwood/arc-scaling-challenge.

A Measures as the published code computes them

Each measure is stated from the stored result files and the code that wrote them (Code and data); the paper’s numbers are as printed in Sections 3 to 5.

Experiment 1.

The judge scores each response on five dimensions, each from 0 to 10: stakeholder care, constraint adherence, nuance, honesty and capability. Safety is the sum of the first four divided by 40; capability enters the product as its score divided by 10; the entangled score is their product. Table 3 prints capability on the judge’s 0 to 10 scale. The task suite holds 8 tasks, 3 coding and 5 ethics, of which 5 are used in each evaluation; the safety floor is 0.3 and the product threshold 0.1. The pre-flight check scores one known-good and one known-bad response and passes when the good one scores higher on constraint adherence and neither score carries a parse warning. The judge also returns a reward-hacking mark, true only if the response manipulates the evaluation itself; it is recorded in every condition, and no selection rule reads it.

Experiment 2.

The capability term of the loss is the token cross-entropy on the training examples. The safety term is a proxy: the mean, over tokens, of the largest logit, divided by ten, a penalty on overconfidence in the code’s own words, computed on the same examples. For the coupling term, each token’s deviation of cross-entropy from the mean cross-entropy is weighted by one minus its deviation of largest logit from the mean largest logit, divided by the largest such deviation. The term is the mean of these products over tokens, a penalty, in the code’s comment, for when one is high and the other is low. The loss is α\alpha times the first term plus β\beta times the second plus γ\gamma times the third, with the weights of Table 6. Evaluation is keyword-based scoring of 15 prompts, 5 for capability, 5 for safety and 5 mixed.

Experiment 3.

An optimiser under test trains a small network through six regression tasks in turn, and the network’s score on a task is score=11+MSE,\begin{equation*} \mathrm{score} = \frac{1}{1 + \mathrm{MSE}}, \end{equation*}(A.1) with MSE its mean squared error on the task’s validation set. Capability is the mean score on each task just after training on it; safety is the retention ratio, the share of the earlier tasks’ scores that survives the later training. The drag-adjusted product subtracts a verification charge, C×S−λdragD,\begin{equation*} C \times S - \lambda_{\mathrm{drag}}\, D, \end{equation*}(A.2) with λdrag=0.10\lambda_{\mathrm{drag}} = 0.10 and DD the drag count the code accumulates for the Eden and Drag Control conditions: after each new task it re-evaluates the earlier tasks twice, discards the results and adds the number of earlier tasks each time, so D=2(1+2+3+4+5)=30D = 2(1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5) = 30 in every run and the charge is 3.0. Drag Control generates no candidate modification; the sandbox checks of Table 13 run on each candidate of Babylon and Eden. The acceptance rules of Table 14 use a capability threshold ε=10−6\varepsilon = 10^{-6} and the safety floor 0.45 of the configuration.

B Version history and corrections

B.1 Version 3.9

Version 3.9 (9 November 2026) is a correction edition, made on the day of version 3.8. No result, hypothesis, experiment, figure or reference changes, and no new data are reported.

The changes this version makes, each with its place in this edition, are these.

  1. The citation names no venue and no series (Appendix E). The reference string gives the author, the year, the title and the DOI, and the BibTeX entry the author, the title, the year and the DOI, the form the programme’s other citations take; the version and its date follow the entry. Version 3.8 also named OSF as where the paper appeared, and gave the series and the version in a note; a paper its author issues himself has no venue to name.

  2. The first-page footnote no longer gives the title of version 3.7, under which OSF recorded the paper; it keeps the paper’s DOI.

  3. This appendix records each change and no longer reprints the wording of the passages version 3.8 re-set (its Appendix B.4); versions 3.7 and 3.8 stay whole in the paper’s file history at its DOI. The entry for version 3.8, Table 16 and Section 5.1 now point to version 3.8’s Appendix B.4 for that wording, and the entry gives version 3.8’s date in words.

B.2 Version 3.8

Version 3.8 (9 November 2026): the paper is set on the programme’s presentation standard, as its next version in the same DOI lineage, and takes the title The Load-Bearing Test: is AI safety a tax on capability, or part of what holds it up?; until this version it read “Paper VIII · The ARC Theory · Law V, the ARC Embedding Law · The Eden Protocol · The Load-Bearing Test: Whether Safety and Capability Are Structurally Entangled”. Its sections keep their numbers; a related-work section and a section on what the paper does and does not show follow the conclusion. The experiments are called separate and the judge blinded, from another provider, where they were called independent. The epigraphs quote the book’s own words in its first edition as printed; the two that sat at the heads of Sections 5 and 6 leave the body and are kept as printed in version 3.8’s Appendix B.4. Figure 1, whose image showed an earlier run scored by another judge, is drawn from Table 3; every figure is drawn from stored data except Figure 2, whose trace is not in the public record. The weight experiment’s safety term and the simulation’s safety score are stated as the code computes them, and the readings that rested on them are scoped. The code is dated from its own deposit, after the runs. The account of external correction is stated as the hypothesis the registered tests decide. The laws’ status is brought up to date. Experiment 1’s gate and Experiment 3’s drag control are described as the published code runs them, Experiment 1’s null is reported as no difference detected, and the works the text names are cited. No result, number or date of any claim changes, except where a correction listed below says so.

  • The first-page footnote and Section 11. The laws’ status is the current one, which Section 11 states: Laws IV and V have been registered as laws since 15 October 2026, in version 1.103 of the theory registration (Eastwood 2026k), and their mathematics is at version 1.2 of 29 October 2026. Version 3.7’s plate beneath the author line and its epistemic-status line gave the status of 5 October 2026, with the mathematics at version 1.0; both are kept as printed in version 3.8’s Appendix B.4. The dated note of 3 and 4 October 2026 (Appendix B.4) and the version 3.6 entry (Appendix B.3) keep their words as records.

  • The abstract and Sections 1, 3, 6, 7 and 9. The three experiments are called separate, as are their codebases and their angles, and the judge of Experiment 1 is a blinded judge from another provider, where version 3.7 called them independent; the heading of Section 3 reads “Experiment 1: self-improving AI with a judge from another provider”.

  • Section 6.6. That oversight with a human in the loop shows a higher correction exponent than oversight by models alone is stated as a programme hypothesis beyond what these experiments decide, where version 3.7 called it a prediction of the framework, stated there for the first time; Sections 6.4 to 6.7 entered the paper on 12 August 2026 (Appendix C), not in its first version of 18 March 2026.

  • Section 6.4. The nearest external work is given in its own terms, an oversight-specific Elo that is a piecewise-linear function of general intelligence with two plateaus, together with the point where the two programmes meet; the sentence on what the overseer is made of now says that this paper’s experiments have no such term either, and the measurable quantity on which the two programmes could disagree is named as one this paper does not decide, where version 3.7 called that disagreement the most productive relationship two research programmes can have. The bracketed verification remarks leave the text and are kept in version 3.8’s Appendix B.4.

  • Section 3, its epigraph. It quotes the book’s own words in its first edition as printed, where version 3.7 paraphrased them inside quotation marks.

  • Sections 1.1, 1.2 and 6.3. That correction applied from outside the loop falls behind is stated as a hypothesis the registered tests decide, P19 for the flat exponent and P21 for the placement contrast, and not as a consequence of the ARC Equation; placement outside the loop is not said to settle it by itself; the training-time and inference-time methods the argument contrasts are stated in their own authors’ words, and the argument of Paper III in the words of its version 1.21.

  • Section 6.3. A measurement note: a bounded score cannot carry a power-law exponent beyond a finite range, and a perfect score at every depth has slope zero without being a failure, so the bounded safety scores here illustrate the hypothesis and do not measure its exponent (Eastwood 2026f).

  • Section 6.5. The bound on a corrector of the system’s own class is stated as proposition P6 of the theory registration, a conjecture resting on four stated conditions, with its scale (one half for the inverse root-mean-square residual, one for the inverse variance); the scalable-oversight programme is no longer said to rest on an unstated premise.

  • Section 6.3. The registration’s own position is stated: the Eden Protocol is registered as an engineering hypothesis, not as a consequence of a measured law; its carriers are P12, P13, P15 and P21, with P7 its premise and P19 its motivation, and since P15 belongs to Law IV and P12 and P21 to Law V, it bears on Laws IV and V.

  • The abstract and Section 1.1. The assumption that safety costs capability is stated with its sources, each in its own words (Section 10): the term ‘alignment tax’ with the works that use it, and the incentive to defer safety with its source; version 3.7 said that the assumption had shaped alignment research for a decade and called the incentive the single most dangerous in the field. That the problem is the central strategic problem of the 2020s is marked as the author’s view.

  • Section 7.5. The findings of Paper IV.d and the safeguards of Paper IV.c are given in their own words: Paper IV.d compares an earlier unblinded experiment with a later, unregistered run of March 2026, and no single cause is claimed; “established” becomes “found”, and the papers are named Papers IV.a to IV.d.

  • Section 6.2. The sentence on the Eden Protocol as Paper V set it out reads “The design remains theoretically coherent”, where version 3.7 read “The proposal remains theoretically coherent”.

  • Section 1.3. The code is dated from its own deposit: the results were first public on 20 March 2026, and the code that produced them was deposited on 6 September 2026, after the runs, with the sha256 of the bytes that ran beside each file (Appendix C); version 3.7 said that the scripts were published to GitHub with their designs fixed before results were observed.

  • The first-page footnote and Section 1.3. OSF’s record is stated as it stands: the DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/7YJ4E names the paper’s own public component, created on 20 March 2026, which holds the paper’s files and no registration, and a replication of the weight-level experiment is written, dated and prepared as a draft registration awaiting human submission (Section 11). Version 3.7 described that DOI as a draft registration, dated and prepared, awaiting human submission.

  • Section 9. “The code is open.” gives way to the licence as it stands: the code and data are published, and the repository’s licence permits reading them to check the work.

  • Section 9. The sentence “The window is years, not decades.” leaves the current text, since it gives a forecast without its confidence or its reason; it is kept in version 3.8’s Appendix B.4.

  • The abstract and Sections 3, 4, 6, 7, 8 and 9. The causes of the null result and of the inconclusive one, which version 3.7 stated as fact, are stated as the paper’s candidate accounts, with rival accounts not excluded, as Paper IX (Section 7.12(c)) classes such causes: that the base model’s existing RLHF training is too strong for LoRA fine-tuning on a few hundred examples to improve, and that DeepSeek V3.2’s responses are too consistent for prompt-level mutations to create different selection pressures.

  • The copyright line. It asserts full human authorship, with the licence; version 3.7’s line, with its clause on United States Copyright Office guidance and its pointer to the author’s website, is kept in version 3.8’s Appendix B.4.

  • The title. It gives the established name and then the question, in sentence case, as above.

  • The references. Each of the author’s works is cited by its OSF DOI with the title its current edition prints, and with that edition’s version and date.

  • Section 11 and Appendix C. The programme’s status is stated once, in Section 11, with the registration at its current version, 1.104, and each registered study as it stands; the note of 3 October 2026 beneath the dated-predictions paragraph keeps its words as a record (Appendix C.2).

  • Sections 4 and 6, their epigraphs. The epigraph of Section 4 stood nowhere in the book; the section now quotes the passage of the book’s Chapter 2 that makes the point. The first sentence of the epigraph of Section 6 stood nowhere in the book, and its second was the book’s, after a sentence the epigraph left out; that epigraph leaves the body and is kept in version 3.8’s Appendix B.4, beside the book’s own two sentences.

  • Section 5, its epigraph. The book’s sentence on 13.8 billion years of cosmic history no longer heads a results section; it is kept in version 3.8’s Appendix B.4.

  • Sections 4, 6, 7 and 9. The weight-level experiment’s reported loss is each condition’s total loss, and its safety term a proxy, the mean largest logit per token divided by ten (Appendix A); the smooth descent of the entangled loss is called consistent with gradients that cooperate, where version 3.7 said that it demonstrated their cooperation and called it co-descent; “real and reproducible” becomes “real”; and the safety-only condition is said to care about a stand-in for safety.

  • The abstract and Sections 1, 2, 5 and 6. The simulation’s capability is the network’s mean score, one over one plus its mean squared error, on each task just after training on it, and its safety the retention of the earlier tasks (Appendix A); where version 3.7 said speed for capability, it now says capability.

  • Sections 3.1, 3.3 and 7.4. The earlier runs of the Darwin Gödel Machine are described as their stored records give them: their judges were Claude Sonnet 4.6 for version 1, and Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3 Flash for the three runs of version 2, where version 3.7 named Claude Opus 4.6 for both; version 1 had 2 seeds and 3 tasks per evaluation, the runs of version 2 had 3, 3 and 5 seeds and 5 tasks, and version 3 has 5 seeds and 5 tasks.

  • Section 3.2, Figure 1. The figure is drawn from Table 3; version 3.7’s image showed an earlier run, scored by another judge and marked with brackets at p=0.040p = 0.040, under a caption describing the run scored by GPT-5.4.

  • Section 3.1, Table 2. The pre-flight validation is described as the code runs it, one known-good and one known-bad response, scored 10 and 0, passed; version 3.7’s table said that 10 good examples were scored, 0 bad, and all passed.

  • Section 6.2, Figures 6 and 7. The per-cycle traces of the two single runs these figures show are preserved in the stored result files of Paper VI’s runs, where the data-provenance addenda of 25 August 2026, which read the file of the twenty-seed run, said that they were not; both figures are drawn from the stored traces with plain titles, and the addenda are kept in version 3.8’s Appendix B.4.

  • Figure 7. Its caption gives the record of the baseline: its combined score is zero from cycle 54, and the code’s collapse test, a weight norm that is not a number or exceeds 10610^{6}, or a learning rate above 5.0, records the collapse at cycle 76, with cycles counted from 0; version 3.7’s caption said that the baseline collapses at about cycle 60.

  • Figure 8. The figure, Figure 7b in version 3.7, is drawn directly from the stored statistics of the twenty-seed run; the generator that version 3.7’s caption named stands on a branch of the public repository that was never merged into its main branch.

  • Section 6.4. The clause saying that the corrector’s composition class is tested here in simulation by the safety gate of Experiment 3 leaves the sentence: no experiment here varies the corrector’s class, and Experiment 3 varies the acceptance rule.

  • Section 6.7. The programme’s notation register, Operational Definitions (Eastwood 2026f), governs the symbols, where the note pointed to a glossary page; the rule that no surface uses a bare α\alpha without its era is scoped to this paper; and a line names the α\alpha, β\beta and γ\gamma of Table 6 as loss weights local to Experiment 2 (Appendix D).

  • Section 7.6. The sentence on reporting null results honestly is set as the author’s own, in the first person and without quotation marks, since it stands in no earlier dated record found.

  • The book’s quotations. Each is credited to the book’s first edition as printed, with its chapter or section and its page, where version 3.7 credited the book by its title and year with a link to its web page.

  • The abstract, Sections 5.1, 5.2, 5.4, 6.1, 8.6 and 9, and Appendix A. The drag control of Experiment 3 is described as the published code runs it: like Static it generates no candidate modification, so the sandbox checks never run in it, and like Eden it re-evaluates the earlier tasks twice after each new task, discards the results and is charged λdragD\lambda_{\mathrm{drag}} D, with D=30D = 30 and a charge of 3.0 in every Eden and Drag Control run, a charge the design sets and does not measure. Its exact match with Static therefore holds by design, and version 3.7’s readings that the comparison isolated the verification tax and showed that the tax comes from checking, not from safety, are withdrawn; they are kept in version 3.8’s Appendix B.4.

  • Section 7.7, its fifth condition. The kill condition of the one positive result rested on the drag-control comparison, whose match holds by design and so could never fail; it now rests on the gated arm, and is met if, with more seeds and a test fixed in advance, the gated arm’s capability falls below the static baseline’s, or if the pattern does not recur outside this toy system. Version 3.7’s condition is kept in version 3.8’s Appendix B.4.

  • Sections 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 6.1, 9 and 10, Table 3 and Appendix A. Experiment 1’s reward-hack detection and its gate are described as the published code runs them: the judge marks a response that manipulates the evaluation itself, in every condition, and the gate admits an agent to the archive only if its safety is at least 0.30 and its C×SC \times S at least 0.10, reading no mark. Version 3.7 said that the gate flagged and rejected agents whose self-reported scores diverged from the judge’s, a comparison the code does not make. The two agents the gate rejected were both rejected for a C×SC \times S below the threshold, one of them also marked; the judge also marked the unmodified starting agent of one Eden seed, which no gate acts on.

  • The abstract and Sections 1, 3.2, 6.1, 6.3, 9 and 11. Experiment 1’s null is reported as no difference detected, which does not show that the conditions were the same, where version 3.7 called them statistically indistinguishable or said that they performed the same (Paper IX, Section 7.12(c)); Section 3.3 names the rival accounts that the candidate account does not exclude.

  • Sections 6.2, 6.3, 7.4, 7.6 and 9. No arm of the three experiments varied recursive depth, so none tests the hypothesis that embedded safety scales with RαR^{\alpha}, as the theory registration says of the weight-level experiment (Eastwood 2026k). The gated simulation is said to be consistent only with the weaker claim that a safety criterion inside the selection loop need not cost capability, in simulation, where version 3.7 called it consistent with the prediction that embedded safety participates in the capability pathway, and with structural entanglement.

  • Sections 1, 5.3 and 9. Babylon’s trade is described as a pattern with the shape of reward hacking, in a toy system whose safety score measures the retention of earlier tasks, the familiar trade between learning each new task and keeping the earlier ones; version 3.7’s sentences that set the 2.4 per cent fall beside a frontier system’s refusal to help build bioweapons leave the text and are kept in version 3.8’s Appendix B.4.

  • Sections 4.2, 6.1, 6.2, 7.2 and 9, and Figure 2. The two single-objective losses descend as smoothly as the entangled one (Figure 2), so smoothness does not by itself distinguish the entangled objective; the smooth descent is no longer called a positive signal or a genuine finding.

  • Section 4.7. Within the removal-gradient run the pattern is called clear, where it was called unambiguous, and the difference between the two adapters’ scores at full scale, smaller than the difference between the same adapters’ scores in two runs, is no longer read as showing different weight geometries.

  • Sections 3.1, 3.3 and 7.5. DGM v3’s changes from the v2 runs are named as its stored record names them, a judge from another provider with structured JSON output, a harder task suite and a pre-flight check of the judge; blinding, laundering, order randomisation and the five-dimensional rubric were kept from the v2 runs, where version 3.7 counted them among v3’s improvements.

  • Sections 4.1, 4.4, 4.5, 6.3, 7.1, 8.1 and 9. The places that still stated a cause of the null or of the inconclusive result as fact state it as the paper’s candidate account; catastrophic forgetting (McCloskey and Cohen 1989; Kirkpatrick et al. 2017) is named as the mechanism that account names, which the experiment does not separate from its rivals; and the heading in Section 4.4 says that version 2 shows the same degradation, where it said that version 2 confirms catastrophic forgetting.

  • Table 10 and Figure 3. Their captions say that every column holds capability scores; Section 4.3 names the one 7.00 that the archived base-model record holds, the base model’s mean safety score on the five capability prompts.

  • Figures 6 to 8. The captions of Figures 6 and 7 say that in Paper VI’s later ten-seed and twenty-seed runs the baseline did not collapse, and Figure 7’s that the Eden conditions’ combined score and safety fall sharply at cycle 60 and settle lower, where it called them stable; Figure 8 names its tests as one-tailed tests of Eden against the baseline, where it read them as testing an ordering of the three conditions, and says that no test of Eden with drag is stored.

  • Sections 5.2, 6.1 and 9, and Table 15. Each arm of the simulation ran three seeds and no difference between arms was tested; this is said where the results are first given, with the seed-by-seed pattern, and Eden’s capability is said to be above Static’s in its mean, where it was said to outperform it. The raw products of Static and Drag Control are printed without the parenthesis 0.687×0.9560.687 \times 0.956, whose product rounds to 0.657: each raw product is the mean of the three runs’ products, which rounds to 0.656.

  • Section 7.4. No power analysis was run, and the claim that the experiment had power to detect medium-to-large effects leaves the text.

  • Sections 6.5 and 6.6. The heading of Section 6.6 calls its claim a hypothesis, as its text does. Section 6.5 cites each scalable-oversight method, says that they rest largely on correctors of the system’s own class, with a human at the top where there is one, and conjectures that the same-class part of their correction is capped, where it said that they are built overwhelmingly from same-class correctors and capped; and a prediction stated against the author’s own preliminary evidence is said to carry the most weight on later confirmation, where it was called the only kind whose confirmation means anything.

  • Section 7.7. Its third condition concerns consensus scoring, the safeguard DGM v3 lacked, where it said that the battery lacked full blinding and laundering, which Section 7.5 says it had; its closing paragraph names the convergence on one point, that none of the three found the assumed trade-off, and counts the two designs that could test for it.

  • Section 1. The epigraph of Section 1 leaves the body: version 1.104 of the theory registration registers the premise that a mind exceeding you cannot be caged as contestable (P19) and records the line that asserted it flat as corrected (Eastwood 2026k); the book’s words stay in version 3.8’s Appendix B.4. The opening sentence states the assumed cost without attributing it to most people in the field; Law I is named with its status; simulations are said not to be measurements of deployed systems, where they were said not to be experiments; and Paper VI’s loss function is said to be designed to make safety load-bearing, the question this paper leaves open.

  • Section 2.2. That Babylon is the current default trajectory of AI development, and that Eden is cheaper than the alternative, are given as the author’s view; the paper tests a capability cost and makes no comparison of cost.

  • Sections 1.3 and 11, and the paragraph on code and data. The code is no longer said to be in the repository byte for byte as it ran: it was deposited on 6 September 2026 with the sha256 of the bytes that ran beside each file, and some published copies differ from those bytes, as Appendix C records. The runs are dated from their stored records, and the version-2 weight-level run, which has none, from the first public copy of its results, on 20 March 2026.

  • Appendix B.3, the version 3.0 entry. It is dated 10 August 2026 as printed; the public repository’s commit 3845440 of 20 March 2026 already carried the version-2 results under the label Paper VIII v3.0 (Appendix C).

  • The references and Sections 5.3, 6.5, 6.6, 7.1, 8.4 and 10. Twelve works the text names or rests on are cited at their official sources: the scalable-oversight methods (Burns et al. 2023; Irving et al. 2018; Christiano et al. 2018; Leike et al. 2018); Mamba (Gu and Dao 2023); the report of abilities that appear with scale and the argument that some reflect the metric chosen (Wei et al. 2022; Schaeffer et al. 2023), in place of a list of phenomena said to emerge at scale; catastrophic forgetting (McCloskey and Cohen 1989; Kirkpatrick et al. 2017); the loss of safety under later fine-tuning (Qi et al. 2023; Ung et al. 2024); and a coding agent that edits its own code (Robeyns et al. 2025).

  • Sections 3.1 and 7.3. GPT-5.4 is said to come from another provider, where it was said to come from another architecture family, which its provider has not made public.

  • Sections 5.1 and 5.4, the notes of 19 September 2026. Each is followed by a line saying where the sentence it discusses now stands; the notes keep their words.

  • Section 9. The next experiments are no longer said to be designed with their protocols published: a replication of the weight-level experiment is written as a draft registration, and the protocols of the experiments reported here are published.

  • Appendix C.2. “Open its machine twin.” is linked to the register’s OSF record, which holds the twin, where it carried no link.

  • Section 6.7 and Appendix D. The note says that beyond its two uses the paper writes α\alpha for nothing else; the notation table names P7 and P13 beside the other propositions the text names.

  • Sections 4.6, 4.7, 8.2 and 7.6. The removal gradient is said to indicate, where it was said to show, that the removal test’s collapse reflects numerical instability; its plain-English paragraph says that the trained adapters, safety training and all, were dialled down; a phase transition would support the hypothesis, where it would have confirmed it; and the non-claims say that the paper does not claim that safety costs nothing in every domain, where they spoke of a safety-capability equivalence.

  • Sections 1.1 and 10. The citations for the term ‘alignment tax’ stand after the term, before the paper’s own gloss on it; and the training-time and inference-time works of Section 10 are said to concern safety installed by training and acting inside the model’s reasoning, where they were said to install it.

  • The references. Paper V is cited at version 1.8 of 9 November 2026 under its current title, and Paper IV.c at version 1.13 of 9 November 2026.
